title: [Unity] Each queued main-thread dispatch allocates about 15 objects, and UnityWebSocketBridge pays that for every received message
body:
## Summary
ExecuteQueuedAsync allocates a TaskCompletionSource, a closure with delegates, a work item and a boxed async state machine per call, and UnityWebSocketBridge.HandleMessage adds closures, a ContinueWith task and a settings clone. This is roughly 14-15 objects per off-main-thread message (counted from code, not measured). A 200 messages-per-second feed produces about 3000 short-lived objects per second, causing frequent GC on IL2CPP mobile.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/MainThreadDispatcher.cs:500`

## Problem
ExecuteQueuedAsync (500-564) allocates per call a TaskCompletionSource and its Task, one closure object with the execute and fail delegates (512-546), a DispatchWorkItem, and the boxed async state machine with its Task (it always suspends on tcs.Task at 563); with a token it adds a closure registration (508-510), where platform.md asks for a static callback with state. UnityWebSocketBridge.HandleMessage (UnityWebSocketBridge.cs:217-236) adds a closure with two delegates, Dispatch/DispatchItem add an object and the RunAction delegate (305, 504), Observe adds a ContinueWith task (346-351), and ExecuteAsync adds the settings clone (MainThreadDispatcher.cs:352). The object count is from reading the code, not measured.

**Failure scenario.** A WebSocket feed of 200 messages per second -> roughly 3000 short-lived objects per second from dispatch plumbing alone, before any payload copy -> frequent GC on IL2CPP mobile. Metrics and quality callbacks take the same path.

## Suggested fix
Give the queue a pooled or struct work item (callback, state, optional completion) with a non-async enqueue path for token-less fire-and-forget callbacks, and let the bridge enqueue one reusable item per message instead of going through the Task-returning ExecuteAsync.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The queue supports a pooled or struct work item with a non-async enqueue path for token-less fire-and-forget callbacks
- [ ] UnityWebSocketBridge enqueues one reusable item per message without going through the Task-returning ExecuteAsync
- [ ] Allocations per dispatched WebSocket message are measured before and after, with a target of at most 2 objects per message in steady state
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix and passes after it (allocation-budget test for the dispatch path)

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `unity-runtime-02` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/unity.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: performance.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Structure confirmed by reading; count not measured. Per off-main-thread message: HandleMessage closure + two delegates (UnityWebSocketBridge.cs:229-235), DispatchItem + RunAction delegate (305, 504), settings clone (MainThreadDispatcher.cs:352), TaskCompletionSource + Task (505-506), closure with execute and fail delegates and a sealed-class DispatchWorkItem (78, 512-546), boxed async state machine + Task because it always awaits tcs.Task (563), plus the ContinueWith continuation task (UnityWebSocketBridge.cs:346-351): about 14-15 objects, more if EnqueueAsync (MainThreadWorkQueue.cs:313, async ValueTask) suspends. The token-registration closure (508-510) does not apply to the WebSocket path (no token passed). No pooled or struct fast path exists. #120 (zero-allocation hot path) lists body transport, H1 parser and H2 lists, not the dispatcher.

title: [Unity] MainThreadDispatcher initialization requires a type-name probe for UnitySynchronizationContext whose captured context is never used
body:
## Summary
IsUnitySynchronizationContext matches SynchronizationContext.Current by type-name substring, and CaptureMainThreadIdentity throws when it fails. The captured context is only read for a metrics boolean; work is delivered through the PlayerLoop/Update drain, never Post. A project that replaces or nulls the main-thread SynchronizationContext makes the dispatcher bootstrap throw and stay Uninitialized, so every Unity helper called from a worker throws for the session.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/MainThreadDispatcher.cs:768`

## Problem
IsUnitySynchronizationContext (768-776) matches SynchronizationContext.Current by FullName.IndexOf("UnitySynchronizationContext"). CaptureMainThreadIdentity(requireUnitySynchronizationContext: true) throws InvalidOperationException when the probe fails (749-755) and is called from the BeforeSceneLoad bootstrap (248), Awake (276) and EnsureInstanceReady (686). The captured _unitySynchronizationContext is only read for a metrics boolean (186) and the null check at 730; work is delivered through the PlayerLoop/Update drain, never through Post. The main thread id could be taken from Thread.CurrentThread in the BeforeSceneLoad hook, which Unity always runs on the main thread. platform.md asks for compile-time selection instead of runtime type probes.

**Failure scenario.** A project sets SynchronizationContext.SetSynchronizationContext(null) or installs its own context on the main thread in an AfterAssembliesLoaded/SubsystemRegistration hook (a known trick to stop awaits from hopping through Unity's context). The dispatcher bootstrap throws 'UnitySynchronizationContext was not available on startup', the state stays Uninitialized, and every Unity helper called from a worker throws 'MainThreadDispatcher is not initialized yet' for the whole session.

## Suggested fix
Record the main thread id unconditionally in the BeforeSceneLoad hook and in Awake, drop the context requirement and the name probe, and keep HasUnitySynchronizationContext (if wanted) as a pure diagnostic.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The main thread id is recorded unconditionally in the BeforeSceneLoad hook and in Awake without requiring a UnitySynchronizationContext
- [ ] HasUnitySynchronizationContext, if kept, is diagnostic only and the name probe no longer gates initialization
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix and passes after it (initialize with a replaced SynchronizationContext, assert dispatch from a worker succeeds)

## Context

title: [Unity] MainThreadDispatcher clones its settings object every frame and on every ExecuteAsync call
body:
## Summary
DrainQueueWithinFrameBudget calls GetSettings(), which clones the settings under a lock, once per frame even when the queue is empty. ExecuteAsync and ExecuteAsync<T> clone again only to read one bool, and each queued WebSocket message adds another clone. Every frame of every game that links TurboHTTP.Unity allocates about 64 bytes (about 3.8 KB/s at 60 fps), against the allocation-free hot-path rule.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/MainThreadDispatcher.cs:932`

## Problem
DrainQueueWithinFrameBudget starts with var settings = GetSettings() (932), and GetSettings returns _settings.Clone() under LifecycleLock (146-152; Clone allocates a new MainThreadDispatcherSettings, MainThreadWorkQueue.cs:99-112). The drain is called once per frame from the PlayerLoop system even when the queue is empty (906-925), in every player because of the unconditional bootstrap (unity-design-02). ExecuteAsync and ExecuteAsync<T> also clone only to read AllowInlineExecutionOnMainThread (352, 427). UnityPerformanceBudgetTests has no idle-allocation budget for the dispatcher.

**Failure scenario.** Every frame of every game that links TurboHTTP.Unity allocates one settings object (about 64 bytes) and takes two locks while idle: roughly 3.8 KB/s of garbage at 60 fps that shows up as a permanent per-frame GC Alloc entry in the profiler, against the project rule that hot paths stay allocation-free. Each queued WebSocket message adds another clone.

## Suggested fix
Keep the validated settings as an immutable snapshot published with Volatile.Write and read the fields directly in the drain and in ExecuteAsync; clone only in the public GetSettings().

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The validated settings are held as an immutable snapshot published with Volatile.Write and read directly in the drain and in ExecuteAsync; only the public GetSettings() clones
- [ ] An idle dispatcher frame allocates 0 bytes and takes no lock beyond the queue check
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix and passes after it (idle-allocation budget in UnityPerformanceBudgetTests for the dispatcher)

## Context

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

The drain is entered once per frame from the PlayerLoop system whenever the state is Ready, before the queue is checked (:911-925, :945), and the dispatcher is created unconditionally at BeforeSceneLoad (:242-250), so every idle frame allocates one settings object and takes LifecycleLock plus the queue lock. ExecuteAsync and ExecuteAsync<T> clone again to read one bool (:352, :427); HandleLowMemory clones too (:997). UnityPerformanceBudgetTests has only a dispatcher.idle_queue_depth budget, no allocation budget. Small per-frame garbage, but permanent and against the allocation rule in CLAUDE.md section 4.

title: [Unity] Low-memory shedding faults MainThreadDispatcher work with OperationCanceledException so WebSocket connected/closed callbacks are dropped
body:
## Summary
HandleLowMemory drops queued user items with a plain OperationCanceledException instead of MainThreadDispatchRejectedException. UnityWebSocketBridge only re-dispatches lifecycle callbacks on the control lane for the rejected exception, so a shed OnConnected or OnClosed callback is discarded despite the documented 'never dropped' guarantee. UnityWebSocketClient then never raises OnDisconnectedEvent for that connection, and texture loads shed by TextureDecodeScheduler look user-cancelled.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/MainThreadDispatcher.cs:1000`

## Problem
HandleLowMemory drops up to LowMemoryDropCount user items with a plain OperationCanceledException (1000-1003); DispatchWorkItem.Fail turns that into tcs.TrySetCanceled (535-541). UnityWebSocketBridge.ObserveDispatchResult maps a canceled dispatch to OnUserLaneFailed(new OperationCanceledException) (UnityWebSocketBridge.cs:359-364), and OnUserLaneFailed only re-dispatches on the control lane when the exception is MainThreadDispatchRejectedException (529-542); everything else falls to 549-552: the callback is discarded and logged. Lifecycle callbacks take the user lane first (HandleConnected 214, HandleClosed 253, DispatchLifecycle 314-320). The bridge documents 'Connected and closed callbacks are never dropped' (44-50) and MainThreadDispatchRejectedException's remarks say drops fault with that type 'so a drop can be told apart from the caller's own cancellation' (MainThreadDispatchRejectedException.cs:42-45); Reconfigure and DropOldest follow it (MainThreadWorkQueue.cs:283-285, 388-392), low memory does not. TextureDecodeScheduler.OnLowMemory faults queued decodes with OperationCanceledException as well (TextureDecodeScheduler.cs:290-291). No test covers low-memory shedding of bridge callbacks.

**Failure scenario.** On a phone under memory pressure Application.lowMemory fires while an OnClosed (or OnConnected) callback is still in the user queue. The callback is shed; UnityWebSocketClient never raises OnDisconnectedEvent for that connection (its only path is the bridge's OnClosed, UnityWebSocketClient.cs:827,846), so reconnect UI waiting for the event never runs. A GetTextureAsync caller in the same frame receives TaskCanceledException although its token was never cancelled, which most callers swallow as a user cancel, so the image silently never appears.

## Suggested fix
Shed with MainThreadDispatchRejectedException (add a LowMemory reason) in both the dispatcher and the texture scheduler, so the bridge's control-lane fallback applies and callers can tell shedding from cancellation. Add a test that sheds a queued lifecycle callback and asserts it still runs.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Low-memory shedding in MainThreadDispatcher and TextureDecodeScheduler faults with MainThreadDispatchRejectedException (new LowMemory reason), distinguishable from caller cancellation
- [ ] A WebSocket connected or closed callback shed by low memory still runs through the bridge's control-lane fallback
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix and passes after it (shed a queued lifecycle callback and assert it still runs; assert the exception type for shed texture decodes)

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `unity-design-09` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/unity.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: architecture.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: HandleLowMemory drops user items with a plain OperationCanceledException (MainThreadDispatcher.cs:1000-1003) via WorkQueue.DropUserWork (MainThreadWorkQueue.cs:518-547, oldest first, default LowMemoryDropCount 128); DispatchWorkItem.fail maps it to tcs.TrySetCanceled (:535-541). UnityWebSocketBridge sends Lifecycle items through the user lane (UnityWebSocketBridge.cs:214, 253, 327), ObserveDispatchResult turns a cancelled task into OperationCanceledException (:359-364), and OnUserLaneFailed re-dispatches on the control lane only for MainThreadDispatchRejectedException (:529-535); otherwise the callback is discarded and logged (:549-552). That contradicts the documented 'Connected and closed callbacks are never dropped' (:48-49) and MainThreadDispatchRejectedException's remark that drops are distinguishable from cancellation. The other drop paths do use the rejected exception (MainThreadWorkQueue.cs:283-285, 388-392, 474-478). One correction: UnityWebSocketClient has a second OnDisconnected path (ReleaseConnectionAsync, UnityWebSocketClient.cs:554-557), but it runs only when the component itself disconnects/reconnects and also uses the sheddable user lane, so a server-initiated close whose OnClosed is shed is still lost. TextureDecodeScheduler.OnLowMemory faults with OperationCanceledException (TextureDecodeScheduler.cs:290-291), so callers see an OperationCanceledException (not TaskCanceledException) without having cancelled. No test exercises low-memory shedding of bridge callbacks. Window is the queue residency at the moment Application.lowMemory fires.

Also reported as `unity-runtime-05` (merged into this issue).

title: [Unity] MainThreadWorkQueue Wait policy keeps timed-out and cancelled waiters queued and counted against MaxPendingWaiters
body:
## Summary
WaitForQueueSpaceAsync completes a waiter on timeout or cancellation but never removes it from the waiter queue; only a freed slot dequeues. The Task.Delay timer is also not cancelled when the waiter is signalled. With the main thread paused and producers retrying, after 2048 attempts new callers get WaiterLimitReached immediately although no live waiter exists.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/MainThreadWorkQueue.cs:370`

## Problem
EnqueueAsync adds a waiter and rejects when _spaceWaiters.Count >= _maxPendingWaiters (370-382). WaitForQueueSpaceAsync completes the waiter on timeout or cancellation (613-641) but never removes it from the queue; only SignalSpaceWaiter_NoLock dequeues, when an item leaves the user queue (675-683). Each wait also starts a Task.Delay timer that is not cancelled when the waiter is signalled (629).

**Failure scenario.** Wait policy with the main thread paused (app in background) and producers that keep retrying: after 2048 attempts every new caller gets WaiterLimitReached at once although no live waiter exists, instead of waiting WaitTimeout; 2048 completed TaskCompletionSources stay referenced until the loop resumes.

## Suggested fix
Remove the waiter (or keep a live-waiter count) when it completes by timeout or cancellation, and cancel the delay when the waiter is signalled.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A waiter is removed, or a live-waiter count is decremented, when it completes by timeout or cancellation
- [ ] The delay timer is cancelled when the waiter is signalled
- [ ] After N timed-out waits with a paused main thread, a new caller waits for WaitTimeout instead of failing with WaiterLimitReached
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix and passes after it (Wait policy test with a blocked drain)

title: [Unity] AdaptiveHandler wraps every response body in CountingResponseBodySource for sample fields nothing reads
body:
## Summary
AdaptiveHandler wraps each non-buffered response body in CountingResponseBodySource and defers the network-quality sample until the body completes. This is done to fill BytesTransferred and TotalDurationMs, but NetworkQualityDetector reads only LatencyMs, WasTimeout and WasSuccess. Every adaptive request pays for a wrapper and a delayed sample with no consumer.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Mobile/AdaptiveHandler.cs:63`

## Problem
OnResponseStartAsync wraps every non-buffered body in CountingResponseBodySource (57-64, the 127-line wrapper in CountingResponseBodySource.cs) and defers the sample until the body completes (94-98), to fill NetworkQualitySample.BytesTransferred and TotalDurationMs (123-129). NetworkQualityDetector reads only LatencyMs, WasTimeout and WasSuccess (NetworkQualityDetector.cs:114-128); BytesTransferred, TotalDurationMs and WasTransportFailure have no reader outside the test seam TryGetLatestSample (rg).

**Failure scenario.** Every streamed or multi-segment response of a client with UseAdaptiveNetworking pays an extra allocation and an interface hop per ReadAsync, and its quality sample is delayed until the consumer finishes or disposes the body, for data that never influences the classification.

## Suggested fix
Record the sample at the response head and drop the wrapper and the unused sample fields, or make the detector actually use throughput.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The sample is recorded at the response head, or the detector consumes the byte and duration fields; no unread sample fields remain
- [ ] CountingResponseBodySource is removed or has a real consumer, and response bodies are not wrapped when adaptive sampling does not need them
- [ ] Existing adaptive detector behaviour for latency, timeout and success is unchanged
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [Mobile] Adaptive detector counts every non-2xx response as failure and uses proportion thresholds with an alpha-0.5 EWMA
body:
## Summary
AdaptiveHandler treats any status outside 200-299 as a failed sample, and NetworkQualityDetector feeds these into EWMAs with alpha 0.5 compared against proportion-style thresholds (success >= 0.99/0.97/0.90). A single 404 or timeout therefore reclassifies the network quality. Adaptive timeouts are then changed for all requests because of one ordinary response.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Mobile/AdaptiveHandler.cs:100`

## Problem
AdaptiveHandler.IsSuccessStatus is statusCode in [200,300) (100-104) and feeds wasSuccess (77, 97). NetworkQualityDetector recomputes three EWMAs with default alpha 0.5 over the window on every sample (NetworkQualityDetector.cs:33, 96-135) and names them _timeoutRatio/_successRatio; Classify compares them with thresholds shaped like proportions: success >= 0.99/0.97/0.90, timeout < 0.01/0.03/0.08 (177-208; NetworkQuality.cs:66-72). With alpha 0.5 a single failed sample puts the success value at 0.5 and it needs four further successes to pass 0.90; a single timeout puts the timeout value at 0.5 >= FairTimeoutRatio, which triggers the immediate demotion to Poor (215-219). Samples older than about seven have no influence, so windowSize 64 only adds a 64-iteration recompute under the lock per request. The project error model treats 4xx/5xx as normal responses.

**Failure scenario.** An API answers 404 for 'no saved game' (or 401 before a token refresh, or 429). Three samples later the quality drops from Good to Fair and timeouts are multiplied by 1.5 for the next several requests; an app that shows a 'poor connection' indicator from GetSnapshot() shows it on a perfect network. One isolated timeout marks the network Poor (timeouts doubled) immediately.

## Suggested fix
Record success for any response that produced a status line (reserve failure for timeouts and transport errors), and either compute true proportions over the window or choose thresholds that match the EWMA; drop the window array if only the EWMA is used.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A response that produced a status line (including 4xx/5xx) is recorded as success; failure is reserved for timeouts and transport errors
- [ ] Classification uses true proportions over the window or thresholds matched to the EWMA, so one failed sample out of a healthy window does not change the quality class
- [ ] Unused window state is removed if only the EWMA is used
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `unity-design-22` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/unity.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: code-smell.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced numerically. AdaptiveHandler.IsSuccessStatus is 200 <= status < 300 (Runtime/Unity/Mobile/AdaptiveHandler.cs:100-104) and is the wasSuccess of every completed response (77, 97), so 3xx/4xx/5xx count as failures. NetworkQualityDetector recomputes EWMAs over the window on each sample with default alpha 0.5 (NetworkQualityDetector.cs:33, 96-135) and Classify compares them with proportion-shaped thresholds (177-208; NetworkQuality.cs:66-72: success >= 0.99/0.97/0.90, timeout < 0.01/0.03/0.08). From a steady Good state one non-2xx gives success 0.5, then 0.75, 0.875 on the next two successes: three consecutive 'Poor' classifications reach _promoteAfterConsecutiveWindows=3 (159-164) and DemoteOneLevel moves Good to Fair; it stays Fair (multiplier 1.5, AdaptiveInterceptor.cs:94-108) until the value passes 0.97 for three more samples. One timeout gives timeout EWMA 0.5 >= FairTimeoutRatio 0.08, so ShouldDemoteImmediately (215-219) sets Poor at once (multiplier 2.0). With alpha 0.5 samples older than about seven contribute under 1%, so the 64-entry window only adds a 64-iteration loop under the lock per request (111-130). No test asserts that a non-2xx status must be a failure sample (AdaptiveByteCountTests.cs:126 covers a transport error after the head). Impact is bounded: opt-in feature, the effect is longer timeouts and a wrong GetSnapshot() quality, not failed requests. Contradicts the project error model (4xx/5xx are normal responses). No open issue.

title: [Mobile] AdaptiveInterceptor clamps default timeouts to [2 s, 30 s], shortening the 45 s mobile default and making infinite 2 s
body:
## Summary
AdaptiveInterceptor multiplies request.Timeout by a quality factor and clamps the result to AdaptivePolicy MinTimeout/MaxTimeout (2 s and 30 s). Only WithTimeout marks a timeout as explicit, so the library default (45 s on iOS/Android, 30 s elsewhere) is clamped, and an infinite default becomes 2 seconds. Slow requests on mobile time out earlier than configured.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Mobile/AdaptiveInterceptor.cs:55`

## Problem
InvokeAdaptiveAsync computes request.Timeout * multiplier and clamps it to [_policy.MinTimeout, _policy.MaxTimeout] (lines 53-57); AdaptivePolicy defaults are 2 s and 30 s (AdaptivePolicy.cs:17-20). Only WithTimeout sets the ExplicitTimeout flag (Runtime/Core/UHttpRequest.cs:330-335); UHttpClientOptions.DefaultTimeout does not. PlatformConfig.RecommendedTimeout is 45 s on iOS/Android players and 30 s elsewhere (Runtime/Core/PlatformConfig.cs:21, 26). Multipliers are 0.8/1.0/1.5/2.0 (lines 94-108). Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan (-1 ms, accepted by the transport's CancelAfter at RawSocketTransport.cs:440) gives max(2000, -1 * m) = 2000 ms. No test exercises the clamp against DefaultTimeout (Tests/Runtime/Mobile/AdaptivePolicySurfaceTests.cs only checks the property surface).

**Failure scenario.** A mobile player calls options.UseAdaptiveNetworking() with defaults: Good quality gives min(30 s, 45 s) = 30 s and Poor gives min(30 s, 90 s) = 30 s, so the feature reduces the default 45 s timeout to 30 s on exactly the networks it is meant to help and never extends it. A client configured with DefaultTimeout = 60 s (the PlatformNotes example) is cut to 30 s; one configured with Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan for long polls times out after 2 s.

## Suggested fix
Clamp relative to the request's own timeout (for example never below it for multipliers >= 1, and MaxTimeout defaulting to a multiple of DefaultTimeout), and pass infinite or non-positive timeouts through unchanged. Add a test with DefaultTimeout above MaxTimeout and with InfiniteTimeSpan.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The adapted timeout is clamped relative to the request's own timeout and is never shorter than the configured default for multipliers >= 1
- [ ] Infinite and non-positive timeouts pass through unchanged
- [ ] MaxTimeout defaults relative to DefaultTimeout rather than a fixed 30 s
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix and passes after it with DefaultTimeout above MaxTimeout and with InfiniteTimeSpan

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `unity-protocol-10` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/unity.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: protocol-impl.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. AdaptiveInterceptor.cs:53-55 computes Timeout * multiplier then Max(MinTimeout) / Min(MaxTimeout); AdaptivePolicy defaults are 2 s / 30 s (AdaptivePolicy.cs:17,20); UseAdaptiveNetworking() with no policy uses those defaults (MobileNetworkingOptionsExtensions.cs UseAdaptiveNetworking). ExplicitTimeout is set only by WithTimeout (UHttpRequest.cs:330-335); DefaultTimeout = PlatformConfig.RecommendedTimeout = 45 s on iOS/Android players (PlatformConfig.cs:21; UHttpClientOptions.cs:40). So mobile default 45 s becomes 30 s at Good/Fair/Poor and 30 s at Excellent (36 -> 30): the feature only shortens. Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan (-1 ms; DefaultTimeout is an unvalidated auto-property, accepted by CancelAfter at RawSocketTransport.cs:440) gives Max(2000, -1*m) = 2000 ms. The clamp itself is documented and tested (AdaptiveInterceptorTests.cs:121-154) but every test sets DefaultTimeout below MaxTimeout; none covers the default interplay or infinite.

title: [Mobile] AdaptiveInterceptor allocates a request copy, three boxed values and a handler per request, plus a state machine per read
body:
## Summary
When the adapted timeout differs from the request's, AdaptiveInterceptor clones headers and the metadata dictionary via CopyWithSharedContent, boxes an enum, a double and an int into context state, and allocates an AdaptiveHandler. Its body wrapper adds an async state machine to each asynchronous read. This is avoidable per-request allocation on mobile.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Mobile/AdaptiveInterceptor.cs:60`

## Problem
Whenever the adapted timeout differs from the request's (any quality other than Good, or a timeout outside MinTimeout..MaxTimeout) the interceptor calls request.CopyWithSharedContent(), which clones the headers and copies the metadata dictionary (AdaptiveInterceptor.cs:58-63, UHttpRequest.cs:514-526). It then boxes an enum, a double and an int into context state (66-68) and allocates an AdaptiveHandler (76). For non-buffered bodies AdaptiveHandler wraps the source in CountingResponseBodySource (AdaptiveHandler.cs:63), whose ReadAsync is an async method around the inner ValueTask with no synchronous fast path (CountingResponseBodySource.cs:58-77). NetworkQualityDetector.AddSample recomputes the EWMA over the whole 64-sample window under its lock for each request (NetworkQualityDetector.cs:96-135).

**Failure scenario.** Adaptive networking on an 'Excellent' network (multiplier 0.8) -> every request pays a header clone, a dictionary copy and about six more objects; a streamed download adds a boxed state machine for each read that completes asynchronously, on top of the per-read allocations #416 and #434 track in Core.

## Suggested fix
Carry the adapted timeout without copying the request, cache the boxed state values, return the inner ValueTask directly when it has completed, and update the EWMA incrementally.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The adapted timeout is carried without copying the request

title: [Mobile] AdaptiveInterceptor restores the original request and disposes its copy only when next() throws synchronously

## Summary
AdaptiveInterceptor publishes a request copy with context.UpdateRequest and restores/disposes it only in a catch around the synchronous call to next. The awaited dispatch task has no try/finally, so an asynchronous failure or cancellation leaves the copy published and undisposed. architecture.md requires restore in finally; DecompressionInterceptor does this correctly.

## Location

## Problem
The copy is published with context.UpdateRequest(requestForNext) (60-62). The copy shares content, so today the effect is limited to the stale context.

## Suggested fix
Wrap the await in try/catch/finally like DecompressionInterceptor.

title: [Packaging] About 1,400 lines of Android/iOS bridge code compile into every platform, with an unguarded static reset hook

## Summary
AndroidJniThread, AndroidBackgroundWorkBridge, AndroidBackgroundExpirySignal, AndroidBackgroundPluginJni, AndroidCleartextTrafficPolicy, IosBackgroundTaskBridge and related types compile on all platforms; only the native call bodies are under #if. Their public constructors succeed elsewhere and return bridges that never acquire a scope, and AndroidAppPauseSource.ResetStaticState runs as a RuntimeInitializeOnLoadMethod on iOS and desktop.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Mobile/Android/AndroidBackgroundExpirySignal.cs:85`

## Problem
Only the native call bodies are behind #if (AndroidBackgroundPluginJni.cs:67-69,83-141; AndroidJniThread.cs:279-303; AndroidCleartextTrafficPolicy.cs:25-34,95-115; IosBackgroundTaskBindings.cs:27-29,67-144). title: [Mobile] Android background networking makes three blocking JNI-thread hand-offs per request for a Java guard map nothing reads
body:
## Summary
With Android background networking enabled, each request calls EnsureInitialized, BeginGuard and EndGuard, each marshalled to the single JNI thread with a WorkItem, closure, PulseAll and a blocked pool thread. On the Java side the guards only put and remove a timestamp in activeGuards, which only currentGuardCount() reads, and no managed code calls that. Throughput of every request is limited by pure overhead.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Mobile/Android/AndroidBackgroundWorkBridge.cs:99`

## Problem
AcquireAsync calls plugin.EnsureInitialized() and plugin.BeginGuard(...) (99), and the scope's dispose calls plugin.EndGuard (141). The platform plugin is AndroidBackgroundPluginOnJniThread (AndroidBackgroundPluginJni.cs:72-81), whose methods each go through AndroidJniThread.Invoke (39-57): the initialized fast path (Volatile.Read at 95-96) sits behind the marshal. Invoke allocates a WorkItem and a closure, enqueues, calls PulseAll and blocks the pool thread in Monitor.Wait until the JNI thread has run the item; every completion PulseAll wakes all waiters (AndroidJniThread.cs:97-123, 186-190). Each call creates an AndroidJavaClass and makes a reflective CallStatic (AndroidBackgroundPluginJni.cs:114-125). On the Java side beginInProcessGuard and endInProcessGuard only put and remove a timestamp in activeGuards (TurboHttpBackgroundPlugin.java:34-44), which only currentGuardCount() reads, and no managed code calls that.

**Failure scenario.** 32 concurrent requests on Android with TURBOHTTP_BACKGROUND_NETWORKING -> 96 serialized JNI round trips, each blocking a thread-pool thread and waking all other waiters, to maintain a map nobody consumes. Request start latency grows with concurrency and the JNI thread becomes a global bottleneck for request dispatch.

## Suggested fix
Drop the per-request Java guard and keep the live-scope count in C#, where the expiry signal already lives; failing that, check initialization before marshalling and cache the class and method IDs so a guard is one cheap call.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The per-request Java guard is removed and the live-scope count is kept in C#, or initialization is checked before marshalling and class/method IDs are cached
- [ ] A request with background networking enabled performs no blocking JNI hand-off on the common path (target: zero per request)
- [ ] Expiry and scope-count behaviour is unchanged
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix and passes after it using a fake JNI thread counting invocations
- [ ] Validated on an Android device or emulator and recorded

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `unity-runtime-19` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/unity.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: performance.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. AcquireAsync calls plugin.EnsureInitialized() and plugin.BeginGuard (AndroidBackgroundWorkBridge.cs:99) and the scope dispose calls plugin.EndGuard (141). The platform plugin is AndroidBackgroundPluginOnJniThread (AndroidBackgroundPluginJni.cs:72-81), which marshals every call, including EnsureInitialized whose Volatile fast path (95-96) sits behind the hand-off (39-48). AndroidJniThread.Invoke allocates a WorkItem (plus a closure/delegate per call), enqueues, PulseAll, and blocks the caller in Monitor.Wait until the single JNI thread ran the item; every completion PulseAll wakes all waiters (AndroidJniThread.cs:97-123, 186-190). Each inner call builds an AndroidJavaClass and a by-name CallStatic (AndroidBackgroundPluginJni.cs:114-125). On the Java side the guard is only a map put/remove (TurboHttpBackgroundPlugin.java:34-44) read solely by currentGuardCount (88-90), which nothing managed calls (rg currentGuardCount = Java only); the bridge itself calls the guard 'advisory' (AndroidBackgroundWorkBridge.cs:145). The single-thread marshalling is a deliberate #328 trade-off (no pool thread attached to the VM) and is sound; the finding is that the marshalled work has no consumer, which holds. Main-thread callers run inline (AndroidJniThread.cs:94-95), so it is 1-3 blocking hand-offs per request depending on where the request starts and ends. Opt-in experimental feature; real cost per call is needs-device-validation.

Also reported as `unity-design-19` (merged into this issue).

title: [Mobile] Background replay is half-implemented: queued requests have no consumer and queued clones are never disposed
body:
## Summary
On background expiry BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor enqueues request.Clone() and throws BackgroundRequestQueuedException saying the request was queued for deferred replay, but nothing in Runtime or Samples calls TryDequeueReplayable and Documentation does not mention it. The queue is not IDisposable, so UHttpClient.Dispose cannot release queued clones with detached body copies, and the WorkManager job is cancelled at dequeue time before any replay is sent.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Mobile/BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor.cs:51`

## Problem
On expiry the interceptor enqueues request.Clone() and throws BackgroundRequestQueuedException('...queued for deferred replay') (114-131). The queue is only read by the public TryDequeueReplayable (51-69); rg finds no caller in Runtime/ or Samples~ and no mention in Documentation~ (PlatformNotes.md:126-155 only says requests are 'queued' and 'handed to WorkManager'). TryDequeueReplayable increments Replayed and calls TryMarkReplayComplete, which cancels the WorkManager job, at dequeue time, before any replay is sent (55-61). The class is not IDisposable, so UHttpClient.Dispose cannot release the queued clones, each of which owns a detached body copy (UHttpRequest.Clone, Runtime/Core/UHttpRequest.cs:159-170). No event tells the app that something was queued.

**Failure scenario.** An app enables UseBackgroundNetworking and is backgrounded during uploads. Callers get BackgroundRequestQueuedException and, reading its message and the docs, expect the library to replay; nothing ever does. Up to MaxQueuedRequests (256) cloned requests with their buffered bodies stay in memory for the client's lifetime; after that further expired requests count as Dropped. An app that discovers TryDequeueReplayable must poll it and has no completion channel back to the original caller.

## Suggested fix
Either implement the replay loop (drain on resume through the owning client, with a result callback and disposal on client dispose) or reduce the feature to what exists: rename the exception/metrics, raise an event with the queued request, document TryDequeueReplayable and the app's responsibilities, and make the interceptor IDisposable so queued clones are released.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Either a replay loop drains the queue through the owning client with a result callback, or the feature is reduced and renamed to what exists with the drain API documented and an event raised when a request is queued
- [ ] Queued clones are disposed when the client or queue is disposed
- [ ] The WorkManager job is cancelled only after replay completes
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `unity-design-17` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/unity.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: architecture.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. On expiry the interceptor enqueues request.Clone() and throws BackgroundRequestQueuedException (Runtime/Unity/Mobile/BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor.cs:114-131) whose message is 'Request was canceled after background expiration and queued for deferred replay.' (BackgroundNetworkingPolicy.cs:13). The queue is read only by the public TryDequeueReplayable (51-69); rg over Runtime/, Samples~ and Documentation~ finds no caller and no mention (only Tests/Runtime/Core/BackgroundNetworkingTests.cs). Docs say requests are 'queued' / 'queued and handed to WorkManager' (Documentation~/PlatformNotes.md, iOS and Android background sections; Modules/Unity.md:84) and never tell the app to drain. TryDequeueReplayable increments Replayed and calls TryMarkReplayComplete, which cancels the WorkManager job, at dequeue time before any replay is sent (55-61; AndroidBackgroundWorkBridge.cs:246-266). The class implements only IHttpInterceptor (line 9), so the client's IDisposable-based component disposal (UHttpClient.cs:775) never reaches the queued clones, each a detached copy (UHttpRequest.cs:159-170); up to MaxQueuedRequests=256 stay referenced for the interceptor's lifetime, after which further expirations count as Dropped (116-117). Scope limit: queuing needs a non-null scope (ShouldQueueOnCancellation, 182-186), i.e. an opted-in TURBOHTTP_BACKGROUND_NETWORKING player or a custom bridge; the feature is documented as experimental. No open issue tracks it: #266 is device validation of begin/end/expiry only, #267 (closed) added the Android expiry signal.

title: [Mobile] Background-expiry cancellation of an unqueued request surfaces as bare OperationCanceledException with no coroutine callback
body:
## Summary
BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor links the caller token with the expiration token, and the transport treats the linked token as the caller's, returning a plain OperationCanceledException. When the request is not queued the interceptor rethrows it, BufferedDispatchBridge turns it into a cancelled task, and CoroutineWrapper then calls neither onSuccess nor onError. The caller never cancelled, contrary to the transport rule from #409 and PlatformNotes.md.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Mobile/BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor.cs:111`

## Problem
InvokeWithBackgroundPolicyAsync links the caller token with scope.ExpirationToken (lines 86-89) and passes the linked token down. RawSocketTransport.MapDispatchAttemptFailure treats that token as the caller's (Runtime/Transport/RawSocketTransport.cs:773, 799-804) and returns OperationCanceledException("Request was cancelled"). The interceptor rethrows it unchanged when QueueOnAppPause is false (line 99-103), the request is not replayable (108-112) or the queue is full (114-118). BufferedDispatchBridge turns a plain OCE into responseCollector.Cancel() (Runtime/Core/Pipeline/BufferedDispatchBridge.cs:81-85), i.e. a canceled task. CoroutineWrapper.RunTaskCoroutine ends on task.IsCanceled without calling onSuccess or onError (Runtime/Unity/CoroutineWrapper.cs:200-201). The transport's own rule is the opposite (#409 comment at RawSocketTransport.cs:794-798: never an OperationCanceledException the caller did not ask for), and PlatformNotes.md:155 says such a request 'fails as it would in the foreground'. Tests/Runtime/Mobile/AndroidBackgroundExpiryTests.cs:87 asserts OperationCanceledException for this case, so the test pins the wrong behaviour.

**Failure scenario.** A POST with a stream body is in flight when the app is paused past the budget. The caller's token is not cancelled, yet await throws TaskCanceledException (indistinguishable from the caller's own cancel), and a SendCoroutine user gets neither onSuccess nor onError: the request disappears silently.

## Suggested fix
When the expiration token (not the caller's) caused the cancellation and the request is not queued, throw a UHttpException (for example NetworkError/Cancelled-by-background with the OCE as inner) or a dedicated typed exception that the buffered bridge reports as a fault, and change the test to assert it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] When the expiration token caused the cancellation and the request is not queued, a UHttpException (or a dedicated typed exception reported as a fault) is thrown with the OperationCanceledException as inner
- [ ] CoroutineWrapper invokes onError in this case
- [ ] AndroidBackgroundExpiryTests line 87 is changed to assert the new behaviour
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `unity-protocol-03` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/unity.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: protocol-impl.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. Interceptor passes the linked (caller + expiration) token down (BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor.cs:86-95); RawSocketTransport.MapDispatchAttemptFailure computes callerCanceled from that token (RawSocketTransport.cs:773) and returns a plain OperationCanceledException (799-804), skipping the #409 branch (794-798). The interceptor rethrows unchanged at cs:99-103, 108-112, 114-118. BufferedDispatchBridge maps an exact-type OCE to responseCollector.Cancel() (BufferedDispatchBridge.cs:82-85), UHttpClient rethrows (UHttpClient.cs:422-428), and CoroutineWrapper.RunTaskCoroutine yield-breaks on task.IsCanceled with no callback (CoroutineWrapper.cs:200-201). Tests/Runtime/Mobile/AndroidBackgroundExpiryTests.cs:87 pins OperationCanceledException. No conversion to UHttpException anywhere on the path. Only reachable with the opt-in experimental background feature (iOS and Android bridges), hence medium.

title: [Mobile] Background replay queues non-idempotent requests that were in flight and possibly fully sent
body:
## Summary
IsReplayable returns true for GET/HEAD, for every method when RequireReplayableBodyForQueue is false, and otherwise whenever the body is replayable, without considering method idempotency or whether request bytes were already written. A POST cancelled mid-flight can be queued and replayed, duplicating a side effect. The HTTP/1.1 stale-connection path documents the opposite rule.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Mobile/BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor.cs:163`

## Problem
IsReplayable (lines 163-175) returns true for GET/HEAD, for every method when RequireReplayableBodyForQueue is false, and otherwise whenever request.Content.Replayability != NonReplayable. Method idempotency and whether the request bytes were already written are not considered. The clone is queued (line 114), handed out by TryDequeueReplayable as 'replayable' (line 51) and registered as deferred work (line 121-123). The HTTP/1.1 stale-connection path in the same library documents the opposite rule ('A POST is never replayed', Documentation~/PlatformNotes.md:48-50).

**Failure scenario.** A POST /purchase with a byte[] JSON body has been received and executed by the server; the response is still in flight when the background budget expires. The interceptor queues the request; the app drains TryDequeueReplayable on resume and sends it again: the purchase is applied twice.

## Spec reference
RFC 9110 section 9.2.2

## Suggested fix
Queue non-idempotent methods only when the caller opted in per request (for example via WithBackgroundReplayKey or an explicit flag), or when the transport can prove no request byte was written; expose on the queued item whether the original may have reached the server.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Non-idempotent methods are queued only when the caller opted in per request or the transport proves no request byte was written
- [ ] The queued item exposes whether the original may have reached the server
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix and passes after it with a POST cancelled after send

title: [Mobile] RequireReplayableBodyForQueue = false can only fail: Clone() throws for a stream body inside the cancellation handler
body:
## Summary
With RequireReplayableBodyForQueue false, IsReplayable accepts any body, then the cancellation handler calls request.Clone(), whose stream body CloneDetachedCore throws InvalidOperationException. The option can only produce an exception inside the handler. All tests set it to true.

- `Runtime/Unity/Mobile/BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor.cs:171`

Remove the option (replayability is a property of the body, not a policy) or gate the clone on the body's replayability and count the request as dropped.

title: [Mobile] BackgroundNetworkingPolicy.GracePeriodBeforeQueue has no effect and the iOS remaining-time native path is unreachable
body:
## Summary
ShouldQueueOnCancellation only evaluates the grace period after the expiration token is already cancelled, and by then the iOS bridge reports a zero remaining budget. The option therefore never changes behaviour, and the native turbohttp_background_time_remaining export and its managed binding are never executed. Integrators who raise the value expect earlier queuing before suspension and get none.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Mobile/BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor.cs:186`

## Problem
ShouldQueueOnCancellation returns false unless scope.ExpirationToken is already cancelled (186), then compares scope.RemainingBudget with the grace period (193-197). On iOS GetRemainingBudget returns TimeSpan.Zero as soon as the expiration token is cancelled (IosBackgroundTaskBridge.cs:129-130), so the comparison is always true and native GetRemainingSeconds / turbohttp_background_time_remaining (Plugins/iOS/TurboHttpBackgroundTaskBridge.mm:160-187, with its dispatch_sync to the main queue) and IosBackgroundTaskBindings.ToRemainingBudget are never executed by library code; RemainingBudget has no other reader (rg). On Android the budget is zero while paused-and-expired and the full budget after a resume (AndroidBackgroundExpirySignal.cs:170-182), so the option only decides a resume race.

**Failure scenario.** An integrator raises GracePeriodBeforeQueue to 10 s expecting requests to be queued earlier before iOS suspends the app; behaviour does not change. The careful DBL_MAX handling for backgroundTimeRemaining (#87) is maintained and reviewed but never runs.

## Suggested fix
Either use the remaining budget before expiry (cancel-and-queue when it drops below the grace period) or delete the option, the native export and the managed binding.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Either GracePeriodBeforeQueue triggers cancel-and-queue while the remaining budget is above zero and below the grace period, or the option, the native export and the managed binding are removed.
- [ ] The chosen behaviour is documented in Documentation~/Modules/Unity.md.
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test in Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the change: with a fake bridge reporting a remaining budget below the grace period, the request is queued before expiry (or the option no longer exists).

title: [Mobile] BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor skips queuing an expired request on Android when the app resumes before the cancellation unwinds
body:
## Summary
ShouldQueueOnCancellation requires the remaining budget to be at or below the grace period even though the expiration token is already cancelled. On Android the budget reads as full again once the app is no longer paused, and the catch block runs asynchronously after the timer cancelled the token. A request cancelled by expiry is then neither queued nor counted in Expired and surfaces as a plain OperationCanceledException.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Mobile/BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor.cs:197`

## Problem
ShouldQueueOnCancellation (lines 177-203) requires scope.RemainingBudget <= GracePeriodBeforeQueue (default 2 s) even though the expiration token is already cancelled. On Android RemainingBudget is AndroidPauseExpirySignal.RemainingBudget (Runtime/Unity/Mobile/Android/AndroidBackgroundExpirySignal.cs:170-182), which returns the full budget (default 5000 ms) whenever AndroidAppPauseSource is not paused. The catch block runs asynchronously after the timer thread cancelled the token (AndroidBackgroundWorkBridge.cs:165-174, 199-212).

**Failure scenario.** Pause, budget expires, the bridge cancels all in-flight requests; the user returns to the app a few milliseconds later, before the requests' catch blocks run. RemainingBudget is 5 s > 2 s, so ShouldQueueOnCancellation returns false: the request is neither queued nor counted in Expired and is rethrown as a plain OperationCanceledException (see unity-protocol-03).

## Suggested fix
Decide from the cause, not from a re-read of the budget: if scope.ExpirationToken is cancelled and the caller's token is not, the scope expired. Drop the RemainingBudget comparison or snapshot the expiry state when the token is cancelled.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A request whose scope expiration token is cancelled while the caller token is not is treated as expired and queued, independent of a later budget re-read.
- [ ] The Expired counter is incremented for that request.
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test in Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix: the fake signal reports a full budget after the token is cancelled and the request is still queued.

## Summary
When a request carries no WithBackgroundReplayKey metadata, GetReplayDedupeKey uses Method + ":" + Uri.ToString(), which includes user info and the query string. The key is stored as WorkManager input data and as the unique work name, and is exposed as the public ReplayDedupeKey. Tokens in URLs (access_token, pre-signed URLs) reach the WorkManager database outside the library's redaction rules.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Mobile/BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor.cs:218`

## Problem
GetReplayDedupeKey (lines 205-220) falls back to request.Method + ":" + request.Uri.ToString() when the request carries no WithBackgroundReplayKey metadata; Uri.ToString() includes userinfo and the query string. The key is passed to deferredBridge.TryEnqueueDeferredWork(replayKey) (line 121-123) and to BackgroundRequestQueuedException (line 128-131, public ReplayDedupeKey). AndroidBackgroundWorkBridge.TryEnqueueDeferredWork forwards it to the plugin (AndroidBackgroundWorkBridge.cs:233), and TurboHttpBackgroundPlugin.enqueueDeferredWork stores it as WorkManager input Data and as the unique work name "turbohttp:" + key (TurboHttpBackgroundPlugin.java:52-58, 99-101), both written to WorkManager's on-disk database. Tests assert the URL form (Tests/Runtime/Mobile/AndroidBackgroundExpiryTests.cs:62 'enqueue:GET:https://example.test/expire').

**Failure scenario.** A GET to https://api.example/v1/items?access_token=SECRET (or a pre-signed URL) is in flight when the Android background budget expires. The token-bearing URL is written to the WorkManager database, where it stays for as long as the job lives (indefinitely, see unity-protocol-01), outside the library's redaction rules.

## Suggested fix
Never derive the default key from the raw URL: use a random id or a SHA-256 of method+URL, and keep the URL only in the in-memory queue. Document that an explicit WithBackgroundReplayKey value is persisted.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The default replay key no longer contains the raw URL (random id or SHA-256 of method and URL); the URL stays only in the in-memory queue.
- [ ] Documentation states that an explicit WithBackgroundReplayKey value is persisted.
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test in Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix: a request to a URL with a query token and user info yields a key and exception property that do not contain the token.
- [ ] Deduplication of identical requests still works with the hashed key.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `unity-protocol-02` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/unity.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: low. Angle: security.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Code is as described: GetReplayDedupeKey falls back to Method + ":" + Uri.ToString() (BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor.cs:218-219), passed to TryEnqueueDeferredWork (121-123) and to the public BackgroundRequestQueuedException.ReplayDedupeKey (128-131; BackgroundNetworkingPolicy.cs:20); the plugin stores it as WorkManager input Data and unique work name (TurboHttpBackgroundPlugin.java:52-58, 99-101). The library's own RedactionPolicy treats URL query values and user-info as sensitive by default (Runtime/Observability/RedactionPolicy.cs:49-70), so this bypasses that rule. Downgraded to low: the WorkManager database is app-private storage, the key is not in the exception Message, and the feature is opt-in experimental; exposure needs root/backup access. Lifetime is unbounded only because of unity-protocol-01.

title: [Unity] PathSafety.ResolvePathWithinRoot accepts the root itself, so the atomic write stages the payload in the root's parent
body:
## Summary
ValidateRelativePath accepts "." and IsPathWithinRoot treats an empty or "." relative path as within the root, so the download target becomes the root directory itself. WriteAtomicAsync creates its temp file as a sibling of the target, which is then outside the root, and writes the body (twice with the copy fallback) before failing with an unrelated IOException. This contradicts the guarantee that nothing leaves Application.persistentDataPath.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/PathSafety.cs:183`

## Problem
ValidateRelativePath accepts "." (lines 41-64) and IsPathWithinRoot returns true when the relative path is empty or "." (182-187), so ResolvePathWithinRoot returns the root directory as the download target. WriteAtomicAsync builds the temp name as a sibling of the final path (CreateTempSiblingPath, 307-313), i.e. <parent of root>/<rootName>.tmp-<guid>, writes the whole payload there (142), fails to promote onto a directory, and SafeCopyPromote writes a second staged copy next to it (275-283) before both are deleted. Reached from DownloadToPersistentDataAsync/DownloadToTempCacheAsync (UnityExtensions.cs:122-136). Tests/Runtime/Unity/UnityPathSafetyTests.cs does not cover ".".

**Failure scenario.** client.DownloadToPersistentDataAsync(url, ".") (or a relative path computed from a server-supplied name that collapses to ".") writes the response body twice into the directory above Application.persistentDataPath before failing with an unrelated IOException, contradicting 'it cannot leave Application.persistentDataPath'.

## Suggested fix
Reject a target equal to the root (and targets ending in a directory separator) in ResolvePathWithinRoot, and assert that the temp sibling is inside the root.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] ResolvePathWithinRoot rejects a target equal to the root and targets ending in a directory separator with an ArgumentException.
- [ ] The temp sibling path is asserted to be inside the root before any bytes are written.
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test in Tests/Runtime/Unity/UnityPathSafetyTests.cs covers "." and fails before the fix.

title: [Unity] PathSafety.WriteAtomicAsync is not atomic by default: a failed replace deletes the destination and temp files are never swept
body:
## Summary
PromoteTempFile swallows every replace failure when RequireAtomicReplace is false (the default) and falls back to SafeCopyPromote, which deletes the existing destination before moving the staged copy. The payload is also written before the integrity check runs, so a crash leaves unverified bytes in a name.tmp-guid file that nothing sweeps. Documentation~/Modules/Unity.md claims the file is written atomically.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/PathSafety.cs:267`

## Problem
PromoteTempFile catches every exception when RequireAtomicReplace is false (the default, line 30) and calls SafeCopyPromote (267-270), which deletes the existing destination (285-288) and only then moves the staged copy (290). The payload is written to disk before ValidateIntegrity runs (142-143); the temp file is removed in finally, but a process kill in between leaves name.tmp-<guid> with unverified content, and nothing sweeps those (UnityTempFileManager's startup sweep only matches turbohttp-audio-*). Documentation~/Modules/Unity.md:53 states 'The file is written atomically.'

**Failure scenario.** On a volume or state where File.Replace fails (destination opened by another reader on Windows, a file system without replace support), the fallback deletes the current file; if the process is killed or the move fails afterwards, the previous good file is gone and only a .tmp- file remains. An ExpectedSha256Hex mismatch combined with a crash leaves the rejected bytes on disk under the destination's name prefix.

## Suggested fix
Validate integrity before writing, make the non-atomic fallback opt-in (or at least never delete the destination before the staged copy is in place), and sweep stale <name>.tmp-* siblings when writing the same destination.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The non-atomic fallback never deletes the destination before the staged copy is in place, or is opt-in.
- [ ] ExpectedSha256Hex is verified before the destination is touched and rejected bytes do not remain under the destination name prefix.
- [ ] Stale <name>.tmp-* siblings of the same destination are removed on the next write.
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test in Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix: a simulated Replace failure followed by a failing move leaves the previous file intact.

title: [Unity] Texture2DHandler validates pixelsPerUnit and TextureOptions only after the download and decode
body:
## Summary
GetSpriteAsync passes pixelsPerUnit to CreateSprite after the texture is downloaded, and GetTextureAsync checks MaxConcurrentDecodes, MaxQueuedDecodes and MaxSourceBytes inside PrepareDecodeInput after the response arrived. A caller bug such as pixelsPerUnit 0 or MaxSourceBytes 0 therefore costs a full download and, for sprites, a main-thread decode before the error is reported.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Texture2DHandler.cs:197`

## Problem
GetSpriteAsync passes pixelsPerUnit straight to CreateSprite after GetTextureAsync finished (205-212), while AsSprite validates pixelsPerUnit > 0 up front (183-189). GetTextureAsync validates TextureOptions (MaxConcurrentDecodes/MaxQueuedDecodes >= 1, MaxSourceBytes > 0) inside PrepareDecodeInput, which runs after SendBufferedAsync (131-140, 401-415, 469-475). platform.md: 'validate cheap arguments before dispatching'.

**Failure scenario.** GetSpriteAsync(url, pixelsPerUnit: 0) or GetTextureAsync with MaxSourceBytes = 0 downloads the whole image (and for the sprite decodes it on the main thread and then destroys the texture) before reporting a caller bug.

## Suggested fix
Validate options and pixelsPerUnit at the top of the public methods, before the request is sent.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] GetTextureAsync and GetSpriteAsync validate pixelsPerUnit and all TextureOptions values before the request is sent and throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException.
- [ ] No request is dispatched when validation fails.
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test in Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix: with a counting transport, invalid options result in zero sent requests.

title: [Unity] Texture and AudioClip finalization uses the droppable main-thread user lane, so a backlog fails downloads that already completed
body:
## Summary
Texture2DHandler and AudioClipHandler queue their final decode steps on MainThreadDispatcher.ExecuteAsync, the 512-item user lane that rejects when full by default. UnityWebSocketBridge puts every message and metrics callback on the same lane. When the main thread stalls and the lane fills, a completed download fails with MainThreadDispatchRejectedException and the fallback decode is rejected too.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Texture2DHandler.cs:263`

## Problem
DecodeScheduledAsync, TryThreadedDecodeAsync and CreateSpriteOwningTextureAsync use MainThreadDispatcher.ExecuteAsync, the user lane (227-230, 263-266, 327-330), as does AudioClipHandler.TryManagedDecodeAsync (AudioClipHandler.cs:289-292). The user lane holds 512 items and rejects when full by default (MainThreadWorkQueue.cs:61-67, 348-352). UnityWebSocketBridge puts every message, metrics and quality callback on the same lane (UnityWebSocketBridge.cs:300-306). In TryThreadedDecodeAsync the rejection is caught as a decoder failure and the fallback is queued on the same full lane (336-348).

**Failure scenario.** The main thread stalls for a second (scene load) while a WebSocket feed delivers more than 512 messages -> the lane is full -> a GetTextureAsync whose download and managed decode already succeeded throws MainThreadDispatchRejectedException and the work is discarded.

## Suggested fix
Finalize assets through a lane that waits (the decode scheduler already bounds how many are in flight) instead of the droppable one, or enqueue them with the Wait policy whatever the global setting.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Asset finalization for textures and audio clips does not fail with MainThreadDispatchRejectedException when the user lane is full; it waits or uses a non-droppable lane.
- [ ] The number of in-flight finalizations stays bounded by the decode scheduler.
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test in Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix: with the user lane filled to capacity, GetTextureAsync completes successfully.

title: [Unity] A MaxPixels violation after a managed decode is treated as a decoder failure and triggers a second full decode on the main thread
body:
## Summary
TryThreadedDecodeAsync throws InvalidOperationException for an image over MaxPixels inside the same try whose catch-all falls back to Unity decode. The image is then decoded again with LoadImage on the main thread, with a full RGBA allocation and a frame hitch, before the limit is finally enforced.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Texture2DHandler.cs:322`

## Problem
TryThreadedDecodeAsync throws InvalidOperationException ('Image exceeds configured MaxPixels limit after managed decode') inside its try (317-325). The catch-all at 336-348 logs 'will fall back to Unity decode' and returns null. DecodeScheduledAsync then runs DecodeTexture on the main thread (258-266), which decodes the same bytes with LoadImage and applies the MaxPixels check only afterwards (522-538).

**Failure scenario.** EnableThreadedDecode with a registered decoder, and an image over MaxPixels whose header the pre-check cannot parse (not PNG or JPEG, or a JPEG without an early SOF) -> decoded once off-thread, rejected, then decoded again by LoadImage on the main thread (full RGBA allocation and a frame hitch) before the limit fails the call.

## Suggested fix
Throw a dedicated limit exception from the post-decode check and let it pass through the fallback catch.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A post-decode MaxPixels violation raises a dedicated limit exception that passes through the fallback catch and fails the call without a second decode.
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test in Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the fix: a test IImageDecoder returning an oversized image results in zero LoadImage fallback invocations.

title: [Unity] Managed image decode always falls back because LoadRawTextureData receives only the base mip level while MipMaps defaults to true
body:
## Summary
CreateTextureFromDecodedImage creates a Texture2D with mipChain set from TextureOptions.MipMaps (default true) but supplies only width*height*4 bytes. Unity requires data for every mip level and throws, the exception is caught in TryThreadedDecodeAsync, a warning is logged and the image is decoded again with LoadImage on the main thread. With a real IImageDecoder and EnableThreadedDecode every image is decoded twice. Reviewer confidence is plausible; confirm in the Editor with a real decoder.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Texture2DHandler.cs:365`

## Problem
CreateTextureFromDecodedImage creates Texture2D(width, height, RGBA32, mipChain: options.MipMaps, ...) and calls LoadRawTextureData(decoded.Rgba32) with exactly width*height*4 bytes (lines 356-365; DecodedImage enforces that length, Decoders/DecodedImage.cs:24-30). Unity requires the raw data to cover every mip level of the texture and throws otherwise; the exception is caught in TryThreadedDecodeAsync (336-348), which logs a warning and falls back to Texture2D.LoadImage. TextureOptions.MipMaps defaults to true (line 21). The only test of the threaded path exercises the fallback (Tests/Runtime/Unity/TexturePipelineV2Tests.cs:44-72).

**Failure scenario.** A project registers a working IImageDecoder through DecoderRegistry.Initialize and sets EnableThreadedDecode = true: every image is decoded twice (managed, then LoadImage on the main thread), a warning is logged per image and the main-thread cost the option was meant to remove stays. Confirm in the Editor with a real decoder; the bundled one is a stub (#158).

## Suggested fix
Create the texture, write level 0 with SetPixelData(data, 0) (or create without mips and generate them), then Apply(updateMipmaps: options.MipMaps); cover it with a test decoder.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A managed-decoded image creates a texture without a failed LoadRawTextureData call: level 0 is written with SetPixelData and mips are generated by Apply when MipMaps is true.
- [ ] No fallback warning is logged for a successful managed decode.
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test in Tests/Runtime/Unity/TexturePipelineV2Tests.cs using a test IImageDecoder fails before the fix.

title: [Unity] TextureOptions carries legacy controls: global scheduler mutation, option alias, unread diagnostics downcast, double copy
body:
## Summary
A per-request TextureOptions can reconfigure TextureDecodeScheduler.Shared once with the first caller winning, MaxSourceBytes duplicates MaxBodyBytes, and RecordDecodeDiagnostics writes four unity.texture.* keys through a downcast to IDictionary that nothing reads. With MaxPixels set the body is also flattened twice. These are API-shape and code-smell issues in a package that has not frozen its API.

## Location
- `Runtime/Unity/Texture2DHandler.cs:399`

## Problem
ApplyLegacySchedulerOptions lets a per-request TextureOptions reconfigure TextureDecodeScheduler.Shared once, first caller wins (399-445), for options documented as 'Legacy' (52-64) in a 1.0.0-pre.1 package. MaxSourceBytes is an 'alias of MaxBodyBytes with Phase 15 naming' (36-45, 86). RecordDecodeDiagnostics casts the IReadOnlyDictionary request metadata to IDictionary to write four 'unity.texture.*' keys (665-679); rg finds no reader in Runtime/, Tests/ or docs, and the write silently stops if Core ever wraps the dictionary. With MaxPixels set, ValidatePixelGuardFromHeader calls GetDecodeBytes (499) and PrepareDecodeInput calls it again (396); TryGetExactArray rejects any array larger than the content (564-578), so a pooled body is copied twice with ToArray.

**Failure scenario.** Two features call GetTextureAsync with different MaxConcurrentDecodes: the second is ignored with a one-time warning. A 20 MB image with MaxPixels set allocates 40 MB of temporary arrays before decode. The diagnostics keys cost four boxed writes per image for no consumer.

## Suggested fix
Remove the legacy scheduler fields and the alias before the API freezes, drop or properly expose the decode diagnostics (RequestContext state instead of a downcast), and compute the decode byte[] once.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The legacy scheduler fields and the MaxSourceBytes alias are removed or marked obsolete before the API freezes.
- [ ] Decode diagnostics are exposed through RequestContext state or removed; no downcast of the request metadata dictionary remains.
- [ ] The decode byte array is computed once per request.
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test in Tests/Runtime/Unity/ fails before the change: two requests with different MaxConcurrentDecodes no longer silently ignore the second.
